prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Walmart Inc." (ticker WMT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "WMT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Walmart Inc.
markets: US general merchandise and discount retail
International retail (Mexico, China, India via Flipkart, Canada)

mission.statement: saving people money so they can live better
mission.source: Walmart corporate website (corporate.walmart.com/purpose), stated as the company's purpose
mission.plain: Walmart exists to sell everyday things cheaply so families have more money left for the rest of their lives.

about.plain: Walmart runs huge stores that sell food, clothes, toys, medicine and almost everything else for a home at low prices. It has about 10,900 stores in 19 countries and about 2.1 million workers. You can also shop on its website and app and get things delivered, sometimes within hours. It also runs Sam's Club, where members buy in bulk.
about.customers: Families and shoppers of every income level, plus small businesses and members of Sam's Club and Walmart+.
about.everyday: The big blue Walmart supercenter in town, with its grocery aisles and pharmacy, is where many Americans do their weekly shopping.

money.plain: groceries, household goods, health and general merchandise
stores and online shopping in Mexico, Central America, Canada, China and India (Flipkart)
bulk goods and fuel for paying club members
Sam's Club and Walmart+ membership fees and other income
ads shown to shoppers on its website, app, stores and TVs; nearly $6.4B a year
fees from outside sellers, delivery services and automated warehouses

result.summary: Walmart has a wide moat built on unmatched purchasing and logistics scale: $713B of revenue and a store within about 10 miles of roughly 90% of Americans let it sell for less than almost anyone and still earn a steady ~4% operating margin. That physical network now doubles as a fast-delivery and advertising platform, with eCommerce up 23% and advertising up 38% in Q2 FY27, which makes the advantage harder to copy, though Amazon and Costco remain formidable.

pricingPower.evidence: Walmart's model is everyday low prices rather than raising prices; during the 2022-2025 inflation and tariff periods it passed through some cost increases while gaining share with higher-income shoppers, and Walmart U.S. comparable sales rose 4.6% in FY2026 with transactions and unit volumes growing. Its real power is over suppliers (cost) rather than over customers (price).

moats.evidence: Walmart is among the most recognised retail brands and is synonymous with low prices; the brand drives traffic but does not let it charge premium prices.
Shoppers can switch to Target, Costco, Aldi or Amazon at no cost; Walmart+ and Sam's Club memberships add only mild stickiness.
Its third-party marketplace and Walmart Connect ad business grow more valuable as more shoppers and sellers join, though the network is still much smaller than Amazon's.

With $713.2B of FY2026 revenue it buys more than any other retailer, spreading distribution, technology and marketing costs over the largest sales base and holding about 21% of US grocery spending (Numerator, 2025).
In many small and rural US towns, a Walmart Supercenter captures enough demand that a second big-box rival cannot earn an adequate return.
Walmart is the incumbent; its store-fulfilled delivery model counters pure-online rivals, but competitors are not structurally prevented from copying it.
Decades of supply-chain, inventory and data know-how, now extended with automated distribution centers and store-based same-day delivery, are difficult to replicate quickly.
Its 4,600-plus US store locations, mostly owned and well placed, act as hard-to-replicate fulfillment nodes within a short drive of most Americans.

customers.evidence: Shoppers return weekly for groceries and Walmart has gained share with higher-income households, but satisfaction surveys such as the American Customer Satisfaction Index usually rank it below Costco, Target and Aldi.

talent.evidence: Walmart is the largest private US employer and has raised wages and launched programmes such as Live Better U (debt-free education) and higher-paid store manager roles, but frontline retail work is still seen as low-paid, with high turnover.

product.evidence: Its offer of lowest prices plus wide assortment and same-day delivery is best in class for value, but it is not considered the best in shopping experience or product quality versus Costco, Target or Amazon.

competitors.name: Amazon.com
competitors.note: E-commerce, marketplace, grocery delivery, membership (Prime vs Walmart+) and retail media advertising

competitors.name: Costco Wholesale
competitors.note: Warehouse clubs versus Sam's Club, groceries and household goods in bulk

competitors.name: Target
competitors.note: Discount general merchandise, groceries and same-day delivery

competitors.name: Aldi
competitors.note: Low-price grocery stores expanding rapidly in the US

competitors.name: Dollar General
competitors.note: Small-format discount stores in rural and low-income areas

competitors.name: BJ's Wholesale Club
competitors.note: Warehouse clubs on the US East Coast versus Sam's Club

competitors.name: H-E-B
competitors.note: Groceries in Texas, a key Walmart market

competitors.name: Publix Super Markets
competitors.note: Groceries in the US Southeast; employee-owned, not listed but files with the SEC

competitors.name: Reliance Retail (Reliance Industries)
competitors.note: Retail and e-commerce in India versus Flipkart

marketShare.measure: share of consumer grocery spend (Numerator, 12 months to Sept 2025)

threats: Amazon's push into same-day grocery and perishables delivery across thousands of US towns
Costco and Aldi winning value-seeking shoppers with higher satisfaction and private labels
Tariffs on imported goods squeezing margins or forcing price rises that hurt its low-price image
Rising wage costs for its 2.1 million associates and possible unionisation
Ultra-cheap Chinese platforms (Temu, Shein) in general merchandise
Execution risk in loss-making or low-margin international bets such as Flipkart in India
Leadership transition from Doug McMillon to John Furner in February 2026

ceo.name: John Furner
ceo.background: Joined Walmart in 1993 as an hourly garden-center associate while studying marketing at the University of Arkansas (Walton College, 1996); later buyer, Walmart China merchandising head, Sam's Club CEO (2017-2019) and Walmart U.S. CEO (2019-2026)

c1.evidence: Walmart leads US retail and grocery with $713B of revenue, but discount retail is a mature industry growing roughly 4-5% a year, not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for the lowest everyday prices and one-stop assortment, backed by unmatched scale and a store-based delivery network that rivals have not been able to copy for decades.

c3.evidence: Walmart is a household name and the default discount retailer in America, though fewer customers would enthusiastically recommend it than would Costco.

c4.evidence: Its purpose of saving people money so they can live better has been emphasised consistently since Sam Walton, and over 10 years it matters for household budgets, but it is a commercial value promise rather than a transformative mission.

c6.evidence: “cheap, convenient, everything, crowded” - the impression is broadly positive on price and convenience but mixed on store experience, wages and its effect on small towns.

c7.evidence: Its addressable market of retail, grocery and retail media is enormous (trillions of dollars), but core retail grows slowly; only e-commerce (+23% in Q2 FY27) and advertising (+38%) ride strong secular trends.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into advertising (Walmart Connect, VIZIO), marketplace, fulfillment services, financial services (OnePay), health and India's e-commerce via Flipkart and PhonePe.

m1.evidence: Furner has pushed a tech-led, AI-powered omnichannel vision with store-fulfilled same-day delivery, but he is a pragmatic operator more than a futurist.

m2.evidence: As a 30-year Walmart lifer who started as an hourly associate, Furner thinks long-term and acts like a steward of Sam Walton's culture, though he is not a founder.

m4.evidence: Having started on the store floor, Furner emphasises associates and customers, including higher pay, better schedules and career paths into store management.

m5.evidence: Walmart's culture of thrift and continuous improvement is strong and has added automation, drone delivery and AI shopping tools, but it is not known as an inventor of breakthrough products.

m6.evidence: Furner is deeply hands-on in merchandising and operations but has a marketing, not engineering, background.

m7.evidence: Furner is regarded as a values-driven, people-focused leader, and Walmart's stewardship of lower prices for working families has broad social benefit, but profit and shareholder returns remain central.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by John Furner at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university could be found.

m8b.evidence: Furner is a low-key, operationally focused executive rather than a famous or flamboyant public personality.

m9.evidence: He turned around Sam's Club (closing 63 weak clubs in 2018 and adding technology) and then led Walmart U.S. to years of comparable-sales gains and e-commerce growth from 2019 to 2026.

m10.evidence: Walmart is famous for frugality dating back to Sam Walton driving an old pickup truck, sharing hotel rooms on business trips and keeping a modest Bentonville head office culture.

c10.evidence: By selling food and essentials cheaply to hundreds of millions of customers each week in 19 countries, it lowers the cost of living for very large numbers of people.

p2.evidence: Running the world's largest retail supply chain efficiently is very hard to replicate and important for affordability, but retailing itself is not technologically hard.

f1.evidence: Total revenue rose every year from $559.2B in FY2021 to $572.8B, $611.3B, $648.1B, $681.0B and $713.2B in FY2026.

f2.evidence: Gross margin on net sales was about flat at 24.3% in FY2021 and 24.2% in FY2026, while operating margin edged up from 4.0% to 4.2% after dipping to 3.3% in FY2023.

f3.evidence: Total debt of $50.4B at July 2026 is well above its $11.5B cash, but it is covered by strong cash flow ($19.7B of operating cash flow in the first half of FY2027) and shareholders' equity is positive at $104.5B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $22.5B in FY2021 to $29.8B in FY2026, but it fell to $20.4B in FY2023 on inventory and markdown problems.

v1.evidence: For an ordinary shopper the reason is simple, the lowest prices on a full basket of groceries and essentials in one trip or delivered the same day, but Costco and Aldi compete closely on value.

v2.evidence: Walmart rarely appears near the top of best-places-to-work lists such as Glassdoor's Best Places to Work, and frontline retail pay and turnover weigh on its reputation as an employer.

c5.evidence: If Walmart disappeared, millions of lower- and middle-income families, especially in rural towns where it is the main grocery and pharmacy option, would pay more and travel further for essentials.
